analysis.one_liner: Replaces cash welfare with capped state block grants, time limits, and cuts to food stamps, Medicaid, and immigrant aid.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee held two hearings on this welfare overhaul, which drew no cosponsors and never came to a vote, dying when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the 60-year-old federal guarantee of cash aid to poor families with children, replacing it with lump-sum block grants to states that generally cut off a family after five years. It also would have imposed work rules and time limits on food stamps, tightened disability benefits for poor children, barred most legal immigrants from federal aid, and terminated the Medicaid program as of October 1, 1997 in favor of capped state funding with less federal oversight. The Senate Finance Committee held hearings in June 1996 but never voted on it, and it expired at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments gain the most: they would get lump-sum federal grants with broad control over eligibility, benefit levels, and work rules for cash assistance, child care, child protection, and food aid, plus an optional block grant replacing the food stamp program. The federal budget gains from capped, predictable spending instead of open-ended matching. Banks and payment-processing companies gain a new market, since the bill directs states to move all benefit distribution onto electronic benefit transfer systems. Charitable and religious organizations gain a new revenue channel, because states could contract with them to run welfare services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State governments, federal budget, benefit contractors

how_it_helps.text: State governments get lump-sum block grants for cash assistance instead of open-ended federal matching, with authority to set their own work rules, time limits, and benefit levels, and to decide how to treat families moving from other states.

States gain an optional food assistance block grant in place of the food stamp program, plus consolidated block grants for child protection, child care, and child and family services, each with fewer federal strings.

States gain flexibility under the Medicaid restructuring division, which would terminate the current Medicaid program as of October 1, 1997 and replace it with capped federal payments that states can spend with latitude over benefits, provider payments, and coverage areas.

The bill directs states to implement electronic benefit transfer systems and amends the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to encourage them, creating a mandated market for banks and payment processors that run benefit cards.
States could contract with charitable, religious, and private organizations to administer and provide welfare services, opening a new funding channel for those groups.

analysis.who_pays: Poor families with children bear the largest cost: the federal guarantee of cash aid ends, families generally lose assistance after five years, and states could cut off an adult's payments for not meeting work rules or cooperating with child support enforcement. Legal immigrants lose access to most federal benefits, including food stamps and Supplemental Security Income. Disabled children face stricter eligibility rules and reviews, with childhood SSI benefits potentially cut off at a redetermination after age 18. Food stamp recipients lose aid after three months in any 36-month period unless working 20 hours a week. Nursing home residents and hospitals face funding risk, because the Medicaid division caps federal payments and ends guaranteed federal matching.
analysis.who_pays_short: Poor families, disabled children, and legal immigrants

drawbacks.text: It ends the individual entitlement to cash aid. Under a capped block grant, a family that loses a job in a recession has no guarantee of help, because state funding is fixed regardless of how many families need it; states could also terminate an adult's share of assistance for not meeting work or child-support cooperation rules.

It cuts food stamps for able-bodied adults, making people ineligible after four months of receiving benefits in a 12-month period unless they worked at least 20 hours a week or participated in workfare — a rule that hits people in areas with few jobs hardest.

It bars most legal immigrants from federal benefits, including Supplemental Security Income and food stamps, and denies the earned income tax credit to workers without a social security number — cutting aid to people who work and pay taxes.

It tightens disability benefits for poor children, discontinuing individualized functional assessments and requiring eligibility redeterminations at age 18 under stricter adult criteria, which would strip benefits from many children with serious conditions.

It terminates the Medicaid program as of October 1, 1997 and caps federal payments, shifting the financial risk of recessions, epidemics, and rising medical costs onto states, hospitals, and nursing homes that depend on Medicaid.

It trims supports for children while cutting the programs that serve them: the child care quality set-aside falls from 20 percent of funds to 3 percent, child abuse prevention programs and criminal background checks for child care providers are abolished, and school lunch, breakfast, and summer feeding programs are pared back.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Proponents argued that time limits and work requirements would push families toward self-sufficiency, and the bill does include child support enforcement tools that would help custodial parents collect what they are owed. But the design tilts heavily toward cutting federal costs: converting guaranteed aid into capped block grants means help disappears exactly when the economy turns down, the immigrant and child disability cuts hit some of the most vulnerable people in the country, and the Medicaid restructuring would end guaranteed federal matching for nursing home care. The savings accrue to the federal budget and to state governments' discretion, not to any new support — the child care quality set-aside is cut from 20 percent to 3 percent even as mothers are pushed into work. On the record in this summary, the costs to poor families far outweigh the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Finance Committee, which held two hearings in June 1996 but never voted to send it to the floor, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator William Roth, the Finance Committee chairman, introduced the bill on May 22, 1996 and it was read twice and referred to his own committee the same day.
The Finance Committee held hearings on June 13 and June 19, 1996 — the only substantive actions the bill ever received.
The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, and after a final round of sponsor remarks on June 27, 1996, no further action was ever taken.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, killing the bill without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, the low-income families, disabled children, and legal immigrants who would have lost aid were better off, since the bill never advanced. The reprieve was brief: a similar welfare overhaul built on the same block-grant, time-limit framework was enacted later in 1996 through a House bill that did reach President Clinton's desk and was signed in August 1996.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred on the bill, and it attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so its support in the record was confined to its sponsor, the Republican committee chairman.

industries.note: The bill hands states lump-sum block grants and broad discretion over cash assistance, food aid, child care, and child protection, freeing them from federal matching rules and detailed mandates. States also absorb new financial risk, since capped funding does not grow when recessions swell the caseload.

The bill mandates that states move benefit distribution onto electronic benefit transfer systems and amends the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to encourage it, creating a government-created market for firms that operate benefit card systems. The mandate guarantees them processing revenue regardless of how recipients fare.

States could contract with charitable, religious, and private organizations to deliver welfare services, channeling public benefit dollars to these groups as the government scaled back direct programs.

The Medicaid division would terminate the current program and cap federal payments, threatening revenue at nursing homes and safety-net hospitals that depend heavily on Medicaid, while giving states new latitude over provider payment rates.

Food stamp time limits, disqualifications, and the optional block grant would shrink food stamp redemptions, reducing sales for stores in low-income neighborhoods. The industry's interest in this bill runs with recipients', since both lose when benefits are cut.
